result.summary: Hesiod continues his farming calendar through the vintage, harvest, threshing and ploughing seasons, tied to the rising and setting of stars. He then turns to sailing, warns Perses about winter storms, tells of his father's migration and his own one sea voyage to Chalcis, and names the safe sailing season.

scenes.title: The farmer's year by the stars
scenes.summary: Hesiod gives star-signs for pruning, harvest, summer rest, threshing, vintage and ploughing.
scenes.stakes: A farmer who misses the seasons risks losing his crop and livelihood.

scenes.title: Winter laying-up of ships
scenes.summary: Hesiod tells Perses to beach his ship in stormy season and recalls how their father fled Cyme poor and settled at Ascra.
scenes.stakes: Ships and cargo may be lost to storms; poverty drove the father to sea.

scenes.title: Hesiod's one voyage
scenes.summary: Hesiod says he sailed only from Aulis to Euboea, where he won a tripod at the games of Amphidamas and dedicated it to the Muses.

scenes.title: The safe sailing season
scenes.summary: Hesiod names the time for sailing and urges a quick return before autumn storms.
scenes.stakes: Sailors risk shipwreck if they linger past the season or if the gods will it.

alias_notes.explanation: Kenning for the snail, not a character.

notable_quotes.reason: Hesiod's bitter description of Ascra, his home village.
Rare autobiographical claim of Hesiod's poetry victory at Chalcis.

analysis.text: Human work must follow the order of nature and the gods; timing through stars and seasons is a form of wisdom and survival.
The passage gives rare personal details: a father's migration from Aeolian Cyme and a poetry prize at Chalcis, valuable evidence for early Greek life and trade.

legacy.text: The poem's farming calendar founded the Greek tradition of didactic agricultural poetry, later reworked by Virgil in the Georgics.

fun_facts.text: Hesiod's mention of crossing from Aulis to Euboea is one of the few passages ancient writers used to date him, via the games of Amphidamas.

language_notes.text: Pandion's daughter was Procne, in myth turned into a swallow. The swallow's arrival signals spring, so pruning must finish before it.
House-carrier is a riddling name for the snail, which climbs plants carrying its shell. Its climbing marks the Pleiades' rising in early summer.
Sirius is the Dog Star, whose rising marks the hottest part of summer.
Biblis wine is a famous kind of wine; its exact origin is uncertain. Zephyr is the fresh west wind.
Demeter's grain: Demeter, goddess of agriculture, stands for grain by metonymy.
Day-sleeper is another riddle-name, meaning a thief who sleeps by day and works at night.
Gifts of Dionysus means wine, since Dionysus was the god of wine and the vine.
The Pleiades setting in late autumn, said to flee the hunter Orion, marks the start of winter storms and the end of the sailing season.
The bilge-plug is a stopper in the hull's bottom; removing it lets rainwater drain out of the beached ship.
"Wings of the ship" means its sails; hanging the rudder "over the smoke" stores it near the hearth to season and preserve the wood.
Aulis was where the Greek fleet gathered, delayed by storms, before sailing against Troy; Hesiod notes his crossing was only a short strait.
Hesiod's tripod prize, a bronze cauldron on three legs, was dedicated to the Muses who, he says, first taught him song on Helicon.
"Many-pegged" describes ships fastened with many pegs or dowels, a compound epithet for a well-built ship.
The summer solstice falls in late June, so the safe sailing period begins about mid-August.

context_notes.text: Hesiod dates the farming year by the risings and settings of stars, as ordinary farmers had no calendar.
Orion is a hunter turned constellation; its rising falls in midsummer, when threshing was done.
Slaves and hired servants were part of an ordinary farm household; Hesiod advises on managing them practically.
Cyme in Aeolis was a Greek city on the coast of Asia Minor; Ascra was a village in Boeotia below Mount Helicon.
Chalcis was a major city on Euboea; Amphidamas, a Chalcidian chief, was honored with funeral games.
Notus is the south wind, associated with late-season rain and storms.

literary_notes.text: Calling the snail 'House-carrier' turns a natural sign into a riddle, a kind of kenning.
Repeating 'dawn' stresses the value of rising early, giving the maxim a driving, proverbial rhythm.
The year 'passes beneath the earth' like a living thing, ending the passage with the cycle's close.
Calling Perses "foolish" gives the advice a scolding, personal tone and presents the poet as a stern, authoritative elder brother.
The balanced contrast of winter, summer and "good at no time" gives a humorous, bitter portrait of Ascra, ending on a deflating climax.
Even good sailing depends on Poseidon and Zeus, reinforcing the poem's view that human prudence works only within the gods' will.
Notus "accompanies" Zeus's rain and "stirs up" the sea, making the wind an active companion of the god.
